analysis.one_liner: Makes big gig companies pay Social Security and Medicare taxes on their contractors' pay.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on December 12, 2019 and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required very large companies that use independent contractors — those with at least $100 million in gross receipts and at least 10,000 contractors a year — to treat that contractor pay like wages for payroll tax purposes. The company would pay the full combined Social Security and Medicare tax (12.4% plus 2.9%) on those payments, and the workers would earn Social Security and Medicare credit for that pay, which they currently do not get from the company. It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and received no further action before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent contractors working at scale for large gig companies. Today, when a company hires a contractor, neither party's employer share goes in as a company contribution; contractors pay their own self-employment tax but get no employer-side contribution. This bill would have made the company pay the full combined tax and given the workers Social Security and Medicare credit for the pay, strengthening their future benefits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gig workers with no employer tax contribution

how_it_helps.text: Companies with at least $100 million in gross receipts and at least 10,000 contractors in a year would have to treat payments to those contractors as wages for employment tax purposes, paying the combined 12.4% Social Security rate and 2.9% Medicare rate instead of the normal 6.2% and 1.45% employer shares.

The workers' pay would count toward Social Security: the bill adds those wage amounts and half the employer tax to the earnings counted under the Social Security Act, so contractors would build benefit credit from work where they currently get none from the company.
Aggregation rules would pull a company's controlled affiliates together as a single employer, making it harder to dodge the thresholds by splitting into subsidiaries.

analysis.who_pays: The covered companies — essentially the very large gig-economy platforms — would owe a new payroll tax of roughly 15.3% on their contractor payments. That cost would likely be passed through partly as lower contractor pay or higher prices, and some companies might respond by reclassifying workers or cutting contractor opportunities.

drawbacks.text: The new payroll tax is a real cost of roughly 15.3% on covered contractor payments, and companies would likely pass part of it back to workers through lower pay or to customers through higher prices, which is the standard way payroll tax costs get distributed.
The thresholds ($100 million in gross receipts, 10,000 contractors) exempt smaller platforms, creating a different tax burden for large and small companies in the same market.

The bill changes only the tax treatment, not the workers' legal status, so contractors would gain Social Security and Medicare credit but would still lack employer-provided benefits like unemployment insurance or a wage floor.
It drew support from only 14 of 231 House Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors, so even within its own party it never built the support needed to move.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is straightforward: workers who spend years as contractors would earn Social Security and Medicare credit from the companies they work for, closing a real gap in retirement coverage. The cost is also real — a new payroll tax of about 15.3% that would land partly on the workers' own pay and on prices. The narrow thresholds blunt both sides: the help reaches only workers at very large platforms, and the tax falls only on those platforms, which makes the bill targeted but also leaves most contractors uncovered.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on December 12, 2019, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Debra Haaland introduced the bill on December 12, 2019 with 14 original cosponsors, all Democrats.
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, and the committee scheduled no hearing, markup, or floor vote; no further action appears in the record.
Because the referral was the last action ever recorded, the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large gig-economy platforms came out ahead: by the bill dying without a vote, they avoided a payroll tax of roughly 15.3% on their contractor payments, while their contractors continue to earn no employer-side Social Security or Medicare contribution from them.

for.name: Rep. Debra Haaland
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require payroll tax withholding on contractors of certain large businesses.

for.name: 14 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no Republicans joined.

against.name: Rep. Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or vote; the bill received no committee action after referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and no committee or floor action ever occurred, so the bill never faced a vote where the partisan split could be measured.

industries.industry: Gig-economy platforms (ride-hailing, delivery, and other large contractor-based businesses)
industries.note: Companies with $100 million or more in gross receipts and 10,000 or more contractors would have owed the full combined 15.3% payroll tax on contractor payments. Their interest in stopping the bill ran against workers', since avoiding the tax is what leaves contractors without employer Social Security and Medicare contributions.
Covered contractors would earn Social Security and Medicare credit on pay they currently receive with no employer tax contribution, improving their future benefits.
Businesses under the $100 million or 10,000-contractor thresholds would face no new tax, giving them a cost advantage over the largest platforms in the same markets.
